source.title: Annual report on education spending in England: 2025–26

total_5_18.label: Total school spending per pupil, all ages 5–18

basis.measure: Core schools budget plus school sixth form funding and wider local authority spending on schools (e.g. SEND transport); IFS's preferred measure

total_5_18.quote: All school spending (including wider spending): £8,400 per pupil (same as in 2010–11)

also.quote: In our view, the measure of total school spending per pupil aged 5–18 (the blue series on Figure 3.3) represents the most comprehensive and consistent measure of the real-terms changes in school spending per pupil.

primary.label: Primary school spending per pupil

basis.measure: Spending by individual schools (actual to 2023–24, projected to 2025–26); excludes central spending by local authorities and multi-academy trusts

also.quote: Actual figures up to 2023–24 are based on spending levels by individual schools. This includes spending on school sixth forms, but excludes central spending by local authorities and multi-academy trusts.

primary.note: 2025–26 is a projection (dashed line on Figure 3.4, p.55), based on mainstream school spending per pupil. Closest national comparator for a school's own spend per pupil from CFR/AAR returns, but those returns are cash and academies' figures exclude trust central spending.

secondary.label: Secondary school spending per pupil

basis.measure: Spending by individual schools (actual to 2023–24, projected to 2025–26); excludes central spending by local authorities and multi-academy trusts

secondary.note: Includes spending on school sixth forms (p.54). 2025–26 is a projection.

secondary_vs_primary_gap.label: How much more secondaries spend per pupil than primaries

basis.measure: Spending by individual schools (actual to 2023–24, projected to 2025–26); excludes central spending by local authorities and multi-academy trusts

secondary_vs_primary_gap.quote: Secondary school spending per pupil in England in 2025–26 is due to be about £7,800, which is 12% higher than in primary schools (£7,000).

also.quote: In the 1980s, secondary school spending per pupil was about 56% higher than primary school spending per pupil. This narrowed to 49% in the 1990s and then to 30% in the 2000s.

total_5_18.label: Total school spending per pupil (5–18): change over time

basis.measure: Total school spending per pupil

total_5_18.quote: Under this measure, total school spending per pupil aged 5–18 fell by 10% in real terms between 2010–11 and 2019–20.

also.quote: Since 2019–20, this measure of spending per pupil has risen by 11% in real terms, largely in line with spending on pupils aged 5–16. As a result, spending per pupil aged 5–18 is now about the same level as it was in 2010–11.

Total school spending per pupil aged 5–18 in England fell by 10% in real terms between 2010–11 and 2019–20. Recent funding increases have reversed these cuts and mean that it is now back to 2010–11 levels.

total_5_18.note: Figure 3.3 (p.53) labels the 2010–11 to 2025–26 change as 0%.

core_schools_budget_per_pupil_5_16.label: Core schools budget per pupil (5–16), the DfE's main measure

basis.measure: Core schools budget per pupil; includes grants for employer pension and National Insurance contributions

core_schools_budget_per_pupil_5_16.quote: This measure of spending per pupil fell by 3% in real terms between 2010–11 and 2019–20, before rising by 12% since 2019–20, and it is now about 9% higher than in 2010–11.

school_spending_per_pupil_5_16_excl_gran.label: School spending per pupil (5–16) excluding pension and National Insurance grants

basis.measure: Planned school spending excluding grants for employer pension and National Insurance contributions

school_spending_per_pupil_5_16_excl_gran.quote: If we exclude these grants, spending per pupil fell by 5% between 2010–11 and 2019–20 and has since risen by 10% in real terms. This leaves spending per pupil about 5% higher than in 2010–11.

also.quote: This drove a 10% real-terms increase in spending per pupil aged 5–16.

mainstream_per_pupil_5_16.label: Mainstream school spending per pupil (5–16), excluding special needs (high needs) spending

basis.measure: Excludes high needs spending and pupils in special schools and alternative provision

mainstream_per_pupil_5_16.quote: Mainstream school spending per pupil has risen by 5% in real terms since 2019–20, about half of the overall rise in school spending per pupil over this period.

also.quote: Furthermore, there has been almost no net real-terms change in mainstream school spending compared with 2015–16.
In fact, mainstream school spending per pupil is currently about the same level it was in 2015–16.

primary_and_secondary_since_2019.label: Primary and secondary spending per pupil since 2019

basis.measure: Spending by individual schools (actual to 2023–24, projected to 2025–26); excludes central spending by local authorities and multi-academy trusts

primary_and_secondary_since_2019.quote: Since 2019, we have seen a recovery in spending per pupil, with 1% per year real-terms growth in primary and secondary school spending per pupil expected between 2019–20 and 2025–26.

primary_2010s.label: Primary spending per pupil in the 2010s

basis.measure: Spending by individual schools (actual to 2023–24, projected to 2025–26); excludes central spending by local authorities and multi-academy trusts

primary_2010s.quote: Primary school spending per pupil actually rose by 6% in real terms between 2010–11 and 2019–20, reflecting the transfer of responsibilities and funding.

secondary_2010s.label: Secondary spending per pupil in the 2010s

basis.measure: Spending by individual schools (actual to 2023–24, projected to 2025–26); excludes central spending by local authorities and multi-academy trusts

secondary_2010s.quote: Secondary schools saw a worse picture, with a 7% real-terms cut over the same period.
secondary_2010s.note: Largely reflects the 28% drop in school sixth form funding per pupil (p.106).

core_schools_budget.label: Core schools budget (government funding for pupils aged 5–16)

basis.measure: Core schools budget: central government funding to councils, trusts and schools for day-to-day spending

core_schools_budget.quote: In 2025–26, the government is set to provide about £65 billion for school funding in England.

also.quote: the total core schools budget has risen between 2019–20 and 2025–26 by about 16% in real terms or by £9 billion in 2025–26 prices. It has also risen by about 25% or £13 billion in real terms since 2010–11.

schools_block.label: Schools block of the National Funding Formula (mainstream schools)
schools_block.quote: By far the largest of these funding streams is the schools block of the National Funding Formula, which totalled about £49 billion in 2025–26.

mainstream_school_budgets.label: Mainstream school budgets
mainstream_school_budgets.quote: funding for mainstream state schools, which totalled about £47 billion in 2025–26.

also.quote: Spending on mainstream school budgets has risen by 8% in real terms since 2019–20, significantly below the overall growth in spending.

total_school_spending.label: Total school spending (5–18, incl. sixth forms and wider council spending)
total_school_spending.quote: we estimate that it is likely to total about £73 billion in 2025–26.

also.quote: Since 2019–20, total school spending has risen by 19% in real terms or £12 billion in 2025–26 prices.

growth_5_16_since_2019.label: Growth in spending on pupils aged 5–16, and how much was pension/NI pass-through
growth_5_16_since_2019.quote: total spending on schools for ages 5–16 grew by £10 billion or 17% in real terms between 2019–20 and 2025–26. However, about £2.3 billion of this growth can be accounted for by additional grants to compensate schools for higher employer pension and National Insurance contributions.

also.quote: If we exclude these grants, total spending grew by about 13% or £7.5 billion between 2019–20 and 2025–26.
Over half of this increase in school funding can be explained by growth in spending on special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

council_overspend_vs_budget.label: Councils' planned school spending above the core schools budget (high needs overspending)
council_overspend_vs_budget.quote: planned spending on schools has exceeded the core schools budget by about £500 million in 2024–25 and by about £900 million in 2025–26. This almost certainly relates to overspending on high needs by local authorities

council_central_spending.label: Council central spending on schools (admissions, place planning, admin)
council_central_spending.quote: This is a small element of overall spending, and fell from about £1 billion in 2019–20 to about £0.7 billion in 2025–26.

also.quote: there is also a much smaller block of funding for central school services (close to £500 million per year)

council_wider_spending.label: Other council spending that benefits schools (SEND transport, assessments)
council_wider_spending.quote: local authorities also spend nearly £4 billion per year on other services that mostly or largely benefit schools and pupils, such as SEND assessments and transport

also.quote: Since then, spending has grown by £1.5 billion or 70% in real terms. This is mostly explained by SEND transport and assessment spending, which has grown by £1.1 billion or more than doubled in real terms since 2019–20.

figure_3_2_changes_since_2019_20.label: Real-terms change since 2019–20 by component of council spending on schools (Figure 3.2)
figure_3_2_changes_since_2019_20.note: Data labels on Figure 3.2; each is also stated in the text on pp.50–52.

staff_share_of_costs.label: Share of schools' costs that are staff costs
staff_share_of_costs.quote: Over 80% of schools’ costs are staff costs.

also.quote: Staff expenditure accounts for around 70% of total spending in further education colleges in England

funding_vs_costs_2024_25_2025_26.label: Mainstream funding per pupil vs school costs, 2024–25 and 2025–26
funding_vs_costs_2024_25_2025_26.unit: percentage points (funding growth below cost growth)

basis.measure: Cash-terms growth in mainstream funding per pupil vs a weighted average of teacher paybill, other staff paybill and non-staff costs (Figure 3.9)

funding_vs_costs_2024_25_2025_26.quote: For 2024–25 and 2025–26, mainstream school funding per pupil (the core schools budget less high needs spending) has been growing by less than overall funding per pupil. This reflects the rapid rises in SEND spending. Partly as a result, mainstream school funding per pupil grew by 2 percentage points less than school costs.
funding_vs_costs_2024_25_2025_26.note: The report does not say whether the 2 points is per year or across both years; Figure 3.9 (p.62) shows expected cost growth above mainstream funding growth in each of the two years (bars are unlabelled, so no exact yearly values are published).

funding_vs_costs_outlook.label: Projected gap between cost growth and funding growth to 2028–29

basis.measure: Scenario where mainstream funding per pupil only rises with general inflation

funding_vs_costs_outlook.quote: we project that actual growth in schools’ costs would exceed funding growth by about 0.5–1 percentage points per year. This would place mainstream schools in a very tight position.

also.quote: If we assume that recommendations for all staff are in line with forecasts for average earnings (around 3% for 2026–27 and about 2% thereafter), then the picture looks tight for schools, with funding per pupil growth lagging costs by about 0.5% per year

However, if average earnings growth (and pay awards) were closer to 3% per year (the average for the period between 2010–11 and 2024–25) and the costs of SEND provision also added 0.25% to cost growth (as has occurred in recent years), then schools’ costs would lag mainstream funding growth by about 1% per year over the next three years

funding_vs_costs_outlook.note: The p.63 wording 'costs would lag mainstream funding growth' means funding lags costs (see p.11).

pay_offer.label: Government's proposed teacher pay offer vs earnings forecast

nff_2026_27.label: National Funding Formula uplift for 2026–27
nff_2026_27.quote: with growth of 2.1% in main factor values in the National Funding Formula confirmed for 2026–27.

core_schools_budget_plan.label: Core schools budget plan to 2028–29

per_pupil_real_change.label: Real-terms change in funding per pupil, 2025–26 to 2028–29

also.quote: This settlement implies a 3% real-terms rise in overall funding per pupil as pupil numbers are expected to fall for the next few years.

per_pupil_real_change.note: The report gives 3% on pp.62 and 66 but 4% on p.54. Use 3% (repeated in the summary).

mainstream_freeze_cash_growth.label: Cash growth in funding per pupil if mainstream spending per pupil is frozen in real terms
mainstream_freeze_cash_growth.quote: Under a real-terms freeze in mainstream school spending per pupil, cash-terms funding per pupil for primary and secondary schools would grow by about 2% per year.

why_schools_go_into_deficit.title: Why schools go into deficit
why_schools_go_into_deficit.text: Most of a school's money goes on people: over 80% of schools' costs are staff costs. So when pay and other costs rise faster than funding, or a school loses pupils and the money that comes with each one, the budget is squeezed quickly and staffing is the only big thing left to cut. In 2024–25 and 2025–26, mainstream school funding per pupil grew by 2 percentage points less than school costs, partly because rising special needs costs took a large share of the extra money. A deficit usually comes from several of these pressures at once, not one bad decision.

one_deficit_year.title: What one year of overspending means
one_deficit_year.text: Spending more than you receive in one year is not the same as being in deficit. Many schools keep savings (a reserve) and plan to use some of it, for example to cover a pay rise before funding catches up, or to keep staff while numbers dip for a year. What matters is the pattern: is the reserve still above zero, and is this the first year of overspending or the third? The IFS makes the same point about further education colleges: a single year of deficit does not necessarily mean serious financial trouble, but repeated deficits are a warning sign. On this site, 'in deficit' means the school's total reserve has gone below zero; 'heading for deficit' means it has overspent for at least two years running and, at that rate, would use up its reserve within about three years.
one_deficit_year.note: The IFS sentence is about colleges; the site definitions come from pipeline/money/status.py.

falling_rolls.title: Falling pupil numbers
falling_rolls.text: Schools are mostly funded per pupil, so fewer pupils means less money. Costs do not fall in step: a class with a few fewer pupils still needs a teacher. Primary schools in England have already lost about 100,000 pupils (3%) between 2019–20 and 2024–25, and are expected to lose over 300,000 more (about 8%) by 2030–31. Secondary numbers are expected to start falling from about 2026–27. The IFS points out that money is only saved if schools actually reduce what they spend, such as staff or the number of schools. That is why a well-run school with falling numbers can still find its budget under pressure.

pass_through_grants.title: Grants that pass straight through
pass_through_grants.text: Not every rise in a school's income is extra spending power. When the government raised what schools pay as employers into staff pensions and National Insurance, it gave schools grants to cover the bill. The IFS describes this as extra money to pay for extra outgoings, with no change in real resources. About £2.3 billion of the growth in school funding between 2019–20 and 2025–26 was this kind of grant. So when a school's income jumps, check whether its staff costs jumped by the same amount: the money may simply have passed through.

send_pressure.title: Special educational needs (SEND) pressure
send_pressure.text: Support for children with special educational needs and disabilities is the fastest-growing part of school spending. About 5.3% of pupils now have an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP), up from just below 3% in the past. A mainstream school is expected to pay the first £6,000 a year of extra support for a pupil from its own budget; the council tops up costs above that from its 'high needs' money. Councils' high needs budgets have run up large deficits, which the Office for Budget Responsibility expects to reach £14 billion by 2028. Since 2019, SEND has taken over half of the increase in school funding. A school with many pupils who need extra support can feel this in its core budget even if it is well run.

academy_central_top_slice.title: Academy trusts' central spending (the 'top-slice')
academy_central_top_slice.text: Academy trusts can keep back part of their schools' funding to pay for things run centrally across the trust, such as administration, buildings or staff shared between schools. This is often called a 'top-slice'. Trusts spent £510 per pupil centrally in 2023–24 (in today's prices), more than double the £240 in 2016–17. Councils spent £180 per pupil centrally on the schools they run in 2023–24. The largest items are administrative and teaching staff employed by the trust. This means an academy's own accounts can look leaner than a council-run school's: some of the money spent on its pupils sits in the trust's accounts, not the school's.

real_terms.title: What 'real terms' means
real_terms.text: £1 buys less each year as prices rise. 'Real terms' figures adjust for this so years can be compared fairly. Like the IFS, this site adjusts using the GDP deflator, the standard measure of economy-wide inflation used for public spending, and shows money in 2025–26 prices. Schools' own costs, mostly pay, can rise faster than general inflation, so a school can be better off in real terms and still feel squeezed.

funding_vs_spending_per_pupil.title: Funding per pupil vs spending per pupil
funding_vs_spending_per_pupil.text: Funding is the money a school receives; spending is what it pays out. The two differ when a school adds to or draws on its savings, and because some money is spent on its pupils by someone else: the council (for example special needs top-ups and transport) or, for academies, the trust's central team. Nationally, the IFS puts total school spending at about £8,400 per pupil aged 5–18 in 2025–26, while spending by schools themselves is about £7,000 per pupil in primaries and £7,800 in secondaries (including sixth forms). Compare a school with the figure for its own phase.

pupil_premium.title: Pupil premium
pupil_premium.text: Pupil premium is extra money for pupils from poorer families: £1,515 a year for each primary pupil and £1,075 for each secondary pupil who has had free school meals in the last six years. The rates were frozen in cash terms from 2015–16 to 2021–22 and are over 16% lower in real terms than in 2015–16.

sixth_form_funding.title: Sixth-form funding
sixth_form_funding.text: Sixth forms are funded separately from the rest of a school, per student. In 2025–26, school sixth forms get about £6,400 per student, compared with about £8,000 in further education colleges. Funding per student in school sixth forms is around 20% lower in real terms than in 2010–11, which is a big reason secondary budgets have been tighter than primary ones.

Is {overseer} giving the school extra help or a loan while it recovers?
How often do governors see the budget forecast, and how close were last year's forecasts to what happened?

What does the budget assume about pay rises and pupil numbers over the next three years?

questions.text: If the gap does not close, what would the school cut first?

questions.text: How many pupils does {name} expect in each year group over the next three years?
questions.why: Primary pupil numbers in England are expected to fall by over 300,000 (about 8%) by 2030–31.

questions.text: Is the school planning to merge classes, share staff or work more closely with another school?
Has the council talked about reducing places, merging or closing schools in this area?

questions.text: Could spare space be let out or shared to bring in income?

high_send.when: Suggested site rule (not from IFS): EHCP share above the national 5.3%, or SEN funding a top-quarter share of income

questions.why: Mainstream schools are expected to fund the first £6,000 a year per pupil from their core budget.

questions.text: Does the council's top-up money arrive on time and cover what the support actually costs?
Is the council's high needs budget in deficit, and could that affect the school's top-ups?
questions.why: Councils' accumulated high needs deficits are forecast to reach £14 billion by 2028.

questions.text: What training do staff get in supporting pupils with special needs?
questions.why: The IFS says reform would likely involve building mainstream schools' ability to support pupils with high needs, for instance through more teacher training.

academy.when: School is an academy or free school

questions.why: Academy trusts spent £510 per pupil centrally in 2023–24 on average.

Can the trust move money between its schools, and has this school given or received any?

questions.text: What is {name}'s {reserve} reserve being kept for, and is there a timetable to spend it?
Is any of it already committed, for example to building work or to cover a planned overspend?
Could some be spent on current pupils without putting future years at risk?

tight.when: status == tight (reserve under 3% of a year's income)

questions.text: With {reserve} in reserve, what would happen if costs rose faster than expected next year?
questions.why: Pay awards are set each year by the government after independent advice; the IFS says the picture is tight for schools if they follow forecast earnings growth.

questions.text: Which costs does {name} expect to rise most next year?
Is the budget relying on one-off grants or fundraising to balance?
How much does the PTA (or friends' association) raise each year, and what does it pay for?

questions.why: Nationally, primaries spend about £7,000 and secondaries about £7,800 per pupil in 2025–26.

school.text: Across England, primary schools are expected to spend about £7,000 per pupil in 2025–26.
Across England, secondary schools are expected to spend about £7,800 per pupil in 2025–26, including sixth forms.
Across England, over 80% of schools' costs are staff costs.
In 2024–25 and 2025–26, mainstream school funding per pupil grew by 2 percentage points less than school costs nationally.
Primary pupil numbers in England are expected to fall by over 300,000 (about 8%) between 2024–25 and 2030–31.
Secondary pupil numbers in England are expected to fall by about 100,000 (4%) by 2030–31, starting from about 2026–27.
On average, academy trusts spent £510 per pupil centrally in 2023–24, money that is not counted in their individual schools' own spending.
Council-run primary schools spend about £400 (6%) more per pupil than primary academies, and council-run secondaries about £300 (4%) more, partly because trusts spend some money centrally.
Pupil premium is £1,515 a year per eligible primary pupil and £1,075 per eligible secondary pupil, over 16% lower in real terms than in 2015–16.
Mainstream schools are expected to fund the first £6,000 a year of extra support for a pupil with special needs from their own budget.
School sixth forms get about £6,400 per student in 2025–26, compared with about £8,000 in further education colleges.
Funding per student in school sixth forms is around 20% lower in real terms than in 2010–11.
About £2.3 billion of the rise in school funding since 2019–20 was grants to cover higher employer pension and National Insurance costs, not extra spending power.

council.text: Councils' special needs (high needs) budgets have been allowed to run deficits since 2019 under a 'statutory override' due to end in 2028; total deficits are forecast to reach £14 billion.
Councils top up a mainstream school's costs for a pupil with special needs above £6,000 a year from their high needs budget.
Council spending on special needs transport and assessments has more than doubled in real terms since 2019–20, up £1.1 billion.
Councils' central spending on the schools they run fell from £230 to £180 per pupil between 2016–17 and 2023–24, while academy trusts' rose from £240 to £510.

council.use_when: la in (Hampshire, Norfolk, Bournemouth Christchurch and Poole)
council.text: Hampshire, Norfolk, and Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole have the largest high needs deficits in England.
Councils can adjust the national funding formula for schools in their area, but cannot make big or complicated changes.
In London, rapid falls in primary pupil numbers over the last 10 years have come with fewer teachers but not much change in the number of schools.
About 5.3% of pupils in England now have an EHCP, up from just below 3% historically.
Independent special school places cost on average over £60,000 a year and take over £2 billion of high needs spending, for only 6% of pupils with EHCPs.

national.text: The core schools budget for England is about £65 billion in 2025–26.
Total school spending per pupil fell by 10% in real terms between 2010–11 and 2019–20 and is now back to its 2010–11 level.
Over half of the increase in school funding since 2019–20 can be explained by growth in spending on special educational needs.
Mainstream school spending per pupil is about the same as in 2015–16 in real terms.
The core schools budget is planned to be flat in real terms to 2028–29; with falling pupil numbers, that is about a 3% real-terms rise per pupil over three years.
The OBR forecasts a £6 billion gap between SEND spending and funding in 2028–29, about 9% of the schools budget.
If mainstream funding per pupil only keeps pace with inflation, school costs are projected to grow 0.5 to 1 percentage points a year faster than funding.
Secondary schools now spend only about 12% more per pupil than primaries, down from about 30% in the 2000s.
Pupil premium rates are over 16% lower in real terms than in 2015–16.
UK public spending on education is about 4.1% of national income, down from about 5.6% in 2010–11.
